title: Intussusception
scenario: A mother brings her child (a few months old) to the ER: URTI 1 week ago, a couple of vomiting attacks for 2 days, passed blood and mucus per rectum, attacks of abdominal discomfort (pulling his legs) that disappear after a while. 430F · 437A · 441A · 442A · 442B · Archive
Picture of a baby with red ("redcurrant-jelly") stool; vomiting, crying, flexing his legs. 436F

imgs.cap: Figure 1: US — target/doughnut sign · Figure 2: contrast enema — coiled-spring appearance

qs.q: Take a (focused) history.
a: Vomiting: amount, frequency, colour (bilious?), blood, projectile?, trigger.
Abdominal pain: colicky, episodic, drawing up the legs; normal between attacks?
Stool: blood & mucus ("redcurrant jelly"); abdominal mass.
Hydration (wet diapers), feeding/hungry, recent URTI/gastroenteritis, known conditions (Meckel's, polyps, HSP, CF).
qs.why: The classic history is episodic colicky pain with legs drawn up and calm between attacks, vomiting, and red-currant-jelly stool, often after a viral illness (lymphoid hyperplasia).
hist: Show severity and the degree of dehydration.
Bilious vomiting means obstruction — needs urgent assessment.
Help separate intussusception from pyloric stenosis and gastroenteritis.
Colicky episodic pain, drawing up the legs
The classic episodes as the bowel telescopes.
Typical of intussusception — the child is calm or lethargic between episodes.
A sausage-shaped mass is the intussusception itself.
Shows how unwell the child is.
Lymphoid (Peyer's patch) hypertrophy acts as a lead point.
Pathological lead points — more likely in older children.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Intussusception.
qs.why: A few-months-old infant with colicky episodes, vomiting and blood/mucus per rectum after a URTI = intussusception.

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: Intussusception, (midgut) volvulus, appendicular mass (also gastroenteritis, Meckel's).
qs.why: Bilious vomiting and abdominal pain in a baby could also be volvulus (an emergency) or an appendix mass/gastroenteritis.

qs.q: What congenital abnormality can cause this condition?
a: Meckel's diverticulum (pathological lead point; most cases are idiopathic — lymphoid hyperplasia).
qs.why: Meckel's diverticulum is the commonest pathological lead point, though most cases are idiopathic (Peyer's patch hypertrophy).

qs.q: What is the best (gold-standard) diagnostic tool, and what would you see?
a: Ultrasound — target / doughnut sign (pseudo-kidney sign longitudinally). If US is not conclusive → contrast enema.
qs.why: Ultrasound is quick, radiation-free and highly accurate: the layered bowel within bowel gives a target/doughnut sign.

qs.q: How accurate is it? (high / moderate / low)
a: High.
qs.why: US sensitivity and specificity approach 98–100% in experienced hands.

qs.q: What is the imaging modality in this picture (figure 2)?
a: Barium / contrast enema (telescoping sign).
qs.why: Contrast introduced per rectum outlining the colon = contrast enema, which can also reduce the intussusception.

qs.q: Describe what you see.
a: Coiled-spring appearance; a filling defect within the bowel lumen (meniscus/claw sign).
qs.why: Contrast meeting the intussusceptum outlines it — a claw/meniscus filling defect with coiled-spring appearance.

qs.q: What is the commonest type?
a: Ileocolic (ileocaecal).
qs.why: The ileum telescopes through the ileocaecal valve into the colon — ileocolic is by far the commonest.

qs.q: What is the initial management?
a: NPO, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesia, NG tube, Foley catheter.
Then reduction enema (air/hydrostatic — barium/water) under fluoroscopic or US guidance.
qs.why: Resuscitate and decompress, then reduce non-operatively with air or hydrostatic enema — successful in most cases without peritonitis.

qs.q: What is your next action if reduction is not successful?
a: Laparotomy and manual (surgical) reduction by "milking"; resection if irreducible or gangrenous.
qs.why: If enema fails (or there is peritonitis/perforation), surgery reduces the bowel manually by squeezing it back, and resects non-viable bowel.

tips.t: 436F: "4 marks with a lot of room — ask about every symptom individually: the vomiting, the crying and the red stool." 441A: most students forgot pain and URTI.

title: Inguinal hernia (paediatric) — reducible · irreducible · strangulated
seen_note: 438A — same as previous files" (indirect inguinal hernia)
scenario: An infant with an inguinoscrotal swelling; last week he became irritable and cried a lot; the swelling is reducible (written station). Old exam
An 18-month-old boy with irritability and vomiting for 6 h and an irreducible inguinoscrotal swelling; the swelling had been coming and going for 2 months. Archive
A picture of a strangulated hernia (427). 427

imgs.cap: Right inguinoscrotal swelling — reducible indirect inguinal hernia Left inguinoscrotal swelling — irreducible hernia

qs.q: What is the abnormal finding in the image?
a: A swelling/bulge in the right (or left) inguinoscrotal region.
qs.why: Describe the side and site of the swelling (inguinoscrotal).

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Right indirect inguinal hernia; (18-month-old) irreducible/incarcerated inguinal hernia.
qs.why: An inguinoscrotal swelling in a child is an indirect hernia; an irreducible painful one in a crying, vomiting toddler is incarcerated.

qs.q: What is the second most common DDx? / possible DDx?
a: Hydrocele.
qs.why: Hydrocele is the main alternative scrotal swelling in children.

qs.q: Mention 3–4 clinical points that differentiate the two conditions.
a: See hydrocele case: get above it?, reducible?, transillumination, cough impulse, inguino-scrotal vs scrotal, silk-glove sign.
qs.why: Get above it, reducibility, transillumination, impulse, extent (inguinoscrotal vs scrotal) and the silk-glove sign separate hernia from hydrocele.

qs.q: List 4 complications.
a: Incarceration, strangulation, bowel obstruction, testicular atrophy (compression of the vessels).
qs.why: The narrow deep ring in infants traps bowel easily — incarceration, strangulation, obstruction, and compression of the cord causing testicular atrophy.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Reducible: elective herniotomy as soon as possible (no mesh in children).
Irreducible: ± sedation & analgesia, attempt gentle manual reduction, repair within 24–48 h; if reduction fails → urgent herniotomy with high ligation of the sac.
qs.why: Paediatric hernias never resolve and incarcerate readily — repair (herniotomy, no mesh) soon after diagnosis; an incarcerated one is reduced and repaired within 1–2 days once oedema settles, or operated urgently if reduction fails.

qs.q: (Strangulated) Give 2 DDx, how to differentiate, and the treatment.
a: Strangulated vs incarcerated hernia — differentiated reliably only in the OR (unless the scrotum is black/red).
Treatment: IV fluids, antibiotics, emergency operation (resect gangrenous bowel) + herniotomy with high ligation (no mesh).
qs.why: Only seeing the bowel separates strangulated from incarcerated; strangulation needs emergency surgery with resection of dead bowel.

title: Malrotation & midgut volvulus (bilious vomiting)
scenario: A 3-month-old boy, healthy until 2 days ago, now vomiting green; dehydrated and sick. 438F · Archive Bilious vomiting (scenario not recalled) — picture of green vomit. Archive
NICU neonate, 1 day old, with vomiting and abdominal tenderness; upper GI study result given. 441F

imgs.cap: Upper GI contrast study — "corkscrew" duodenum/jejunum Bilious (green) vomit on the baby's clothes

qs.q: Take a history.
a: Vomiting: onset, frequency, colour (bilious), projectile?; abdominal distension, passage of meconium/stool, blood per rectum; feeding, wet diapers (hydration); antenatal US, prematurity.
qs.why: The colour of the vomit is the key: bilious vomiting means obstruction distal to the ampulla; meconium, distension and blood per rectum help localise it.
hist: Early onset suggests a congenital cause.
Bilious vomiting = obstruction distal to the ampulla — malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
Projectile non-bilious vomiting suggests pyloric stenosis instead.
Little distension suggests proximal obstruction; marked distension suggests distal.
Delay suggests Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus.
Bowel ischaemia — a late, ominous sign of volvulus.
Antenatal findings (polyhydramnios, double bubble) suggest atresia; prematurity matters for management.

qs.q: Give 4 DDx of bilious vomiting in a neonate.
a: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, duodenal/jejunal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus, imperforate anus, (intussusception — less likely at this age).
qs.why: Neonatal bilious vomiting has proximal causes (malrotation, atresias) and distal ones (Hirschsprung, meconium ileus, anorectal malformation).

qs.q: What is the most serious diagnosis to include or exclude? / What is the diagnosis?
a: Malrotation with midgut volvulus.
qs.why: Bilious vomiting is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise — the whole midgut can die within hours.

qs.q: What is the diagnostic tool?
a: Upper GI contrast series.
qs.why: Upper GI contrast shows the position of the duodenojejunal flexure — the gold standard for malrotation.

qs.q: What is the radiological feature seen in this image?
a: Corkscrew sign (also: dilated proximal duodenum — "bird's beak"; duodeno-jejunal flexure right of the midline; absent C-loop).
qs.why: A twisted duodenum/jejunum spiralling down = corkscrew sign; a DJ flexure right of the spine means malrotation.

qs.q: Which part of the bowel is affected?
a: Answer given: ileocaecal.
qs.why: Volvulus twists the whole midgut around the SMA; the narrow mesenteric base is near the ileocaecal region in malrotation.

qs.q: If the diagnostic tool is not available, what is your next step?
a: (Open) exploratory laparotomy.
qs.why: If imaging can't be done and volvulus is suspected, laparotomy can't wait — delay risks losing the bowel.

qs.q: If the diagnosis is confirmed, what is your management? (emergency setting)
a: NPO, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, NGT decompression, Foley catheter.
Emergency surgery: untwist (counter-clockwise), assess viability, Ladd's procedure.
qs.why: Resuscitate and decompress quickly, then emergency laparotomy — time equals bowel.

qs.q: What are the two steps you will do in surgery? / Name the operation.
a: Untwist the bowel and assess viability → Ladd's procedure (divide Ladd's bands, widen the mesentery, appendicectomy, place small bowel on the right & colon on the left).
qs.why: Untwisting (counter-clockwise) restores blood flow; Ladd's procedure (divide bands, widen the mesentery, appendicectomy, non-rotation position) prevents recurrence.

qs.q: What are the consequences if the management is delayed?
a: Bowel ischaemia/gangrene, perforation, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, septic shock, short- bowel syndrome, multi-organ failure, death.
qs.why: Ischaemic midgut becomes gangrenous → perforation, sepsis, acidosis and death; survivors may lose most of the small bowel.

qs.q: Name the syndrome caused by resection of a large amount of bowel.
a: Short-bowel syndrome.
qs.why: Loss of most of the small bowel leaves too little absorptive surface — short-bowel syndrome.

notes.t: In midgut volvulus the whole midgut (from the duodenum to the mid-transverse colon) twists around the SMA axis.

title: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism)
scenario: A mother brings her 6-month-old boy to the clinic saying he has had this condition since birth (picture). 430A · 435 · Archive

qs.q: What is the abnormality you see?
a: Hypoplastic right (430A: left) hemiscrotum.
qs.why: An empty, underdeveloped hemiscrotum means the testis never descended into it.

qs.q: Mention 4 differential diagnoses.
a: Undescended testis, retractile testis, ectopic testis, testicular agenesis/vanishing testis, testicular atrophy.
qs.why: An empty scrotum can be undescended, retractile (can be brought down), ectopic (off the path), or absent/atrophic.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Undescended (right/left) testis.
qs.why: An empty hypoplastic hemiscrotum since birth = undescended testis.

qs.q: Any investigations (laboratory or imaging) for diagnosis?
a: No — it is a clinical diagnosis. (Impalpable testis → diagnostic laparoscopy.)
qs.why: UDT is diagnosed by examination; ultrasound doesn't reliably find impalpable testes — laparoscopy does (diagnostic and therapeutic).

qs.q: How would you treat, and when?
a: Wait for spontaneous descent until 6 months; then standard orchidopexy at 6–12 months (palpable → inguinal/open orchidopexy; impalpable → laparoscopic).
qs.why: Spontaneous descent is unlikely after 6 months; orchidopexy at 6–12 months reduces the risks of infertility, malignancy (and allows self-examination), torsion and trauma.

tips.t: Don't say "empty" on inspection — say hypoplastic; you can only say empty after palpation.

a: Preserve fertility, reduce risk of malignancy (allow examination), torsion and trauma, psychological reasons.

qs.q: Take a history.
a: Most important: projectile, non-bilious vomiting after feeds; hungry baby after vomiting ("hungry vomiter"); dehydration (number of wet diapers); weight gain; first-born male, family history.
qs.why: A first-born boy at 2–8 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting who is hungry after vomiting is the classic pyloric stenosis story.
hist: The pylorus is obstructed above the ampulla, so the vomit has no bile.
The "hungry vomiter" — the baby is otherwise well and wants to feed again.
Poor weight gain shows the duration and severity.

qs.q: Do the physical examination.
a: Palpable pyloric "olive" (RUQ/epigastrium after a test feed), visible gastric peristalsis (left → right), signs of dehydration.
qs.why: The hypertrophied pylorus is felt as an "olive" after a test feed, and gastric peristalsis is visible from left to right.

qs.q: What investigations will you order?
a: Labs: CBC, coagulation, cross-match, blood gas; electrolytes → hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (the doctor asked which abnormalities).
Imaging: ultrasound (pyloric muscle thickness ≥ 3–4 mm, length ≥ 15–16 mm).
qs.why: Loss of gastric acid causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; ultrasound measuring pyloric thickness and length confirms the diagnosis.

qs.q: What is your management?
a: Resuscitation (ABCD), IV fluids to correct dehydration & electrolytes first, NPO + NGT, Foley catheter.
Definitive: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy (once electrolytes are corrected).
qs.why: Pyloric stenosis is not a surgical emergency — the alkalosis must be corrected first (it causes post-op apnoea), then pyloromyotomy.

qs.q: Describe what you do in pyloromyotomy. How is it different from pyloromyectomy?
a: Pyloromyotomy: longitudinal incision through the hypertrophied pyloric muscle down to (but not through) the mucosa, which bulges; nothing is removed. Pyloromyectomy: a strip of muscle is excised.
qs.why: Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy splits the thick muscle down to the mucosa so the lumen opens, without removing tissue or opening the mucosa.

qs.q: Why does the patient have metabolic alkalosis, hypochloraemia and hypokalaemia? What happens in the kidney? (only one track)
a: Vomiting of HCl → loss of H⁺ and Cl⁻ (alkalosis); volume depletion → aldosterone ↑ (acts on the distal tubule/collecting duct) → Na⁺ retained in exchange for K⁺ and H⁺ → hypokalaemia and paradoxical aciduria.
qs.why: Vomiting HCl causes alkalosis and hypochloraemia; dehydration activates aldosterone, which saves sodium by excreting K⁺ and H⁺ — hypokalaemia and a paradoxically acid urine.

title: Hydrocele (vs inguinal hernia)
scenario: A 6-month-old boy brought by his mother because of a scrotal mass present since birth. Archive Picture of an infant with a scrotal swelling. 439A

imgs.cap: Large scrotal swelling — hydrocele (transilluminates) Infant with a scrotal swelling (439A, similar image)

qs.q: Describe what you see.
a: Scrotal swelling (side), skin normal, testis not separately seen; you can get above it.
qs.why: Describe side, skin and whether you can get above the swelling — that separates hydrocele (can) from hernia (can't).

qs.q: Take a detailed history.
a: Since birth?, change in size with crying/during the day, reducibility, pain/irritability, vomiting (obstruction), redness, trauma, prematurity.
qs.why: Ask about onset, variation in size and reducibility (communicating hydrocele vs hernia) and symptoms of incarceration.
hist: Congenital hydrocele or hernia through a patent processus vaginalis.
Change in size with crying or during the day
Variation in size means a communicating hydrocele or hernia.
A hernia reduces; a non-communicating hydrocele doesn't.
Suggest incarceration of a hernia — an emergency.
Increases the risk of hernia and incarceration.

qs.q: Mention 2 differential diagnoses.
a: Hydrocele, indirect inguinal hernia.
qs.why: A scrotal swelling in an infant is either a hydrocele (fluid) or an indirect hernia (bowel) — both through a patent processus.

qs.q: How do you differentiate hydrocele from indirect inguinal hernia? (4 signs)
a: Hydrocele: can get above it, not reducible (communicating may empty slowly), transilluminates, no cough impulse, purely scrotal, baby comfortable, constant size.
Hernia: can't get above it, reducible, cough/cry impulse, inguino-scrotal, silk-glove sign (thick cord), baby may be irritable, appears with crying/straining.
qs.why: A hydrocele is purely scrotal (get above it), fluid-filled (transilluminates) and not reducible; a hernia extends from the canal (can't get above it), reduces and has an impulse.

qs.q: What is the aetiology?
a: Patent processus vaginalis allows peritoneal fluid into the scrotum.
qs.why: A narrow patent processus vaginalis lets only peritoneal fluid into the tunica — a communicating hydrocele.

qs.q: Mention 2 complications if left untreated.
a: Haematocele after trauma, testicular atrophy, infection.
qs.why: Untreated hydroceles may bleed after trauma (haematocele), become infected, or, when large, compress the testis.

qs.q: What is the appropriate management? / When do you operate?
a: Observe until ~2 years (most resolve spontaneously); persistent → surgery: ligation of the patent processus vaginalis at the deep inguinal ring (inguinal herniotomy approach).
qs.why: The processus usually closes by 1–2 years, so observe; persistent hydroceles are treated by ligating the processus through the groin (not by scrotal aspiration).

a: Communicating and non-communicating.

title: Acute appendicitis (child)
scenario: A 10-year-old boy with sudden severe RLQ pain for 24 h, vomiting 3–4 times and mild fever; lying still, slightly dehydrated, marked RLQ tenderness with guarding. Archive

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Acute appendicitis.
qs.why: Migratory RLQ pain, vomiting, low-grade fever and localised guarding in a 10-year-old = acute appendicitis.

qs.q: What is the next important investigation, and the expected specific finding?
a: CBC — leukocytosis with neutrophilia.
qs.why: Leukocytosis with neutrophilia supports the clinical diagnosis.

qs.q: What are the 2 groups of organisms, and an antibiotic for each?
a: Gram-negative bacteria → cefuroxime; anaerobes → metronidazole.
qs.why: A mixed gut infection — cefuroxime covers Gram-negatives, metronidazole covers anaerobes.

qs.q: Name 3 essential management elements before surgery.
a: NPO, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesia (NGT if needed, Foley if low urine output).
qs.why: Children dehydrate quickly and perforate early — resuscitate, give antibiotics and analgesia before theatre.

qs.q: From the history, mention ONE symptom and ONE sign specific to appendicitis.
a: Symptom: periumbilical pain shifting to the RLQ. Sign: Rovsing's sign (rebound tenderness).
qs.why: Pain migrating from the umbilicus to the RLQ (visceral → parietal) and Rovsing's sign are characteristic.

qs.q: How would you differentiate appendicitis from acute pyelonephritis and gastroenteritis? (1–2 each)
a: Pyelonephritis: dysuria, high fever, renal-angle tenderness, urinalysis (WBC, bacteria, nitrite).
Gastroenteritis: vomiting & diarrhoea, travel/food history, vomiting precedes pain (pain first in appendicitis), no RLQ tenderness.
qs.why: Urinary symptoms, renal-angle tenderness and an abnormal urinalysis point to pyelonephritis; diarrhoea with vomiting before pain and no localised tenderness point to gastroenteritis.

qs.q: He presents after a week with worse RLQ pain, high fever and higher WBC — what does he have, and how do you confirm it?
a: Appendicular abscess / appendix mass → CT with contrast.
qs.why: Late presentation with a tender mass and high fever = appendix mass/abscess; contrast CT distinguishes them and guides drainage.

title: Foreign-body ingestion
scenario: Two X-rays of children with swallowed foreign bodies (Figure 1 & Figure 2). Archive

imgs.cap: Figure 1: coin in the oesophagus (AP & lateral) · Figure 2: object in the stomach
Foreign-body ingestion — management by site and type

qs.q: What is the best investigation (modality) for such a case?
a: Answer given: rigid endoscope (X-ray AP + lateral localises it; endoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic).
qs.why: X-rays localise radio-opaque objects; endoscopy both confirms and removes an impacted oesophageal foreign body.

qs.q: Mention two other sites where a foreign body can get stuck in the oesophagus.
a: Upper oesophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus), aortic arch crossing, lower oesophageal sphincter.
qs.why: Foreign bodies lodge at the three physiological narrowings of the oesophagus: cricopharyngeus, aortic arch/left bronchus, and the LES.

qs.q: How do you manage the 1st case (Figure 1 — oesophagus)?
a: NPO, IV fluids, antibiotics if signs of infection → remove endoscopically (must be removed).
qs.why: An object stuck in the oesophagus can cause perforation or erosion (especially batteries) — it must be removed endoscopically.

qs.q: How do you manage the 2nd case (Figure 2 — stomach)?
a: Leave it and follow up — 90 % pass spontaneously — unless symptomatic or it is a
battery/magnets (must be removed).
qs.why: Once past the oesophagus, most smooth objects pass spontaneously — observe; batteries, multiple magnets, sharp objects or symptoms need removal.

a: Sharp objects: wait unless evidence of perforation; batteries must be removed. Complications: bleeding, perforation, infection, stricture.
